"""
Purpose  
To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance.

Introduction  
Structured radiology reporting is essential for clear communication and quality assurance, yet variability in report formats and content can hinder consistency and patient care. Automated tools that standardize report structure and flag quality issues may improve reporting practices. This study aims to address these challenges by developing and evaluating a multi-agent AI system for structuring and quality assurance of radiology reports.

Materials and Methods

Dataset and Study Design  
This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024 at a single institution. Reports were selected consecutively from routine clinical practice without exclusion criteria. The dataset comprised approximately 22,270 sentences.

AI System Development

System Architecture  
A locally deployed multi-agent AI system was developed, consisting of specialized agents with distinct roles. The structuring agent segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level. This was achieved using a hybrid approach: pattern-matching rules (regular expressions) were used to identify anatomical terms and section headers, and these outputs were further processed by locally run large language models (LLMs).

LLM Selection, Training, and Fine-Tuning  
The LLMs were based on open-source transformer architectures, specifically Llama 2. Llama 2 was selected due to its strong performance on medical text tasks, open-source availability, and compatibility with secure local deployment, which is essential for maintaining patient data privacy. The model was fine-tuned on a corpus of 5,000 de-identified radiology reports from the institution, which included a range of modalities and anatomical regions. Annotation for fine-tuning involved manual labeling of sentences with anatomical section assignments and identification of quality issues by two board-certified radiologists, with consensus adjudication for disagreements. Fine-tuning involved supervised learning with annotated examples, using a learning rate of 2e-5 and early stopping based on validation loss. The models were deployed on secure local servers to ensure data privacy and compliance.

Quality Assurance Agents  
The system included several QA agents: (1) a section mismatch agent that detected inconsistencies between the Findings and Impression sections, (2) an intra-section consistency agent that identified contradictions within sections, (3) a gender-anatomy conflict agent that flagged gender-specific anatomical inconsistencies, and (4) a critical findings agent that checked for documentation of communication regarding critical findings. Agents operated in sequence, with the output of the structuring agent serving as input for the QA agents, and each agent’s output was passed to the next for further analysis.

Evaluation Process

Report Selection  
The evaluation phase was conducted separately from system development. Two board-certified radiologists independently evaluated a subset of 45 reports that had been restructured and flagged by the system. The 45 reports were selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation of different types of flagged issues and anatomical regions.

Evaluation Criteria  
Each radiologist reviewed the reports using the following criteria: (1) accuracy of anatomical structuring (correct assignment of sentences to anatomical sections), (2) retention of original clinical content (no loss of clinically relevant information), (3) absence of fabricated information (no addition of content not present in the original report), and (4) overall QA performance. Radiologists applied these criteria by directly comparing the original and restructured reports side-by-side, noting any discrepancies in section assignment, missing or added information, and the appropriateness of QA flags.

QA Performance Rating  
QA performance was rated as "excellent" (no errors and all issues correctly flagged), "good" (minor errors or missed flags not affecting clinical interpretation, such as a sentence assigned to a neighboring but clinically similar anatomical section), or "fair" (significant errors or missed issues that could impact clinical care, such as omission of a critical finding or misassignment leading to potential misinterpretation).

Ambiguity Handling  
Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and the nature of disagreements was recorded to identify potential system limitations. Ambiguous cases included sentences at anatomical boundaries (e.g., “Findings at the diaphragm”) or with unclear references (e.g., “No acute abnormality”). For example, a sentence like “No acute abnormality” could be interpreted as pertaining to the lungs, abdomen, or both, depending on context. In one illustrative case, a sentence describing "findings at the diaphragm" was discussed: one reviewer assigned it to the lung bases, while the other assigned it to the upper abdomen. Consensus was reached by referencing the predominant clinical context and institutional reporting guidelines, ultimately assigning the sentence to the section most relevant to the clinical question. Such examples highlight the importance of context and institutional conventions in resolving ambiguity.

Evaluation Metrics  
Inter-rater agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa statistic, which quantifies the level of agreement between two raters beyond chance (values between 0.61–0.80 indicate substantial agreement; a value of 1.0 indicates perfect agreement, and 0 indicates agreement equivalent to chance). Cohen’s kappa was chosen because it accounts for agreement occurring by chance and is widely used for categorical data in medical studies, aligning with the study’s goal of assessing the reliability of categorical structuring and QA decisions.

Results

System Performance  
The multi-agent AI system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 reports (14.1% of 638), most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%).

Radiologist Evaluation and Interpretation  
In the radiologist evaluation of 45 reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on 12 (27%), yielding a Cohen’s kappa of 0.62. In this context, a kappa of 0.62 indicates substantial agreement between reviewers, suggesting that the system’s structuring decisions were generally reliable but that some subjectivity remains, especially in borderline cases. Disagreements primarily involved borderline cases of anatomical section assignment (e.g., sentences describing findings at anatomical boundaries such as the diaphragm) and interpretation of ambiguous sentences (e.g., statements like "no acute abnormality" without clear anatomical reference). During evaluation, ambiguous cases were discussed in detail, with reviewers referencing clinical context and standard reporting conventions to reach consensus. For example, if a sentence could reasonably belong to either the lung bases or upper abdomen, reviewers considered the predominant clinical context and the institution’s reporting guidelines. These disagreements highlight the inherent subjectivity in anatomical section assignment and the challenges posed by ambiguous language, which can impact the system’s reliability in edge cases. All disagreements were resolved through consensus discussion. Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" in 28 reports (62%), "good" in 10 reports (22%), and "fair" in 7 reports (16%). Minor errors included, for example, a sentence about the adrenal glands being placed in the kidney section, while significant errors included missing a critical finding flag or misassigning a sentence in a way that could alter clinical interpretation. In clinical practice, these results suggest that the system can reliably standardize most reports and flag quality issues, but human oversight remains important for ambiguous or complex cases.

Limitations  
The use of reports from only 15 radiologists at a single institution may introduce bias related to individual reporting styles, institutional conventions, and local terminology, potentially limiting the diversity of language and structure encountered by the AI system. This could affect the system’s ability to generalize to reports from other institutions or radiologists with different styles, possibly resulting in reduced accuracy or missed quality issues when applied to more varied datasets. The retrospective design and single-institution dataset may further limit generalizability, as results could be influenced by local reporting practices and the small number of radiologists.

Conclusion

A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow, demonstrating favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. To address current limitations, future work will include a prospective validation phase, planned for the next 12 months, in which the system is integrated into clinical workflows and its performance is monitored in real time. Additionally, we plan to expand the dataset to include reports from at least three additional institutions and a larger, more diverse group of radiologists, with a target of 10,000 reports by the end of the next year. To improve handling of ambiguous language and linguistic variability, future iterations will incorporate advanced NLP techniques such as context-aware transformer-based models trained on multi-institutional data, and consensus-based rules for anatomical section assignment. For example, the system will use contextual embeddings to better disambiguate sentences at anatomical boundaries and implement rule-based overrides for institution-specific conventions. Active learning approaches will be implemented, where ambiguous cases are automatically flagged for human review, and the resulting feedback is used to iteratively refine the model. Milestones for these improvements include: (1) multi-institutional data collection (months 1–4), (2) model retraining and validation (months 5–8), and (3) prospective clinical integration and monitoring (months 9–12). These steps aim to improve the system’s handling of linguistic variability and ambiguous cases. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.
